opus-5.5.text:
I think of them as complementary, and honestly as something of a testing ground. When we put out our Responsible Scaling Policy, part of the idea was that nobody really knew yet what good regulation for frontier AI should look like. The technology is moving fast, the risks are uncertain, and if you try to write detailed rules too early, you risk locking in the wrong things. Voluntary frameworks let companies try out concepts like capability thresholds, the evaluations that tell you when you've crossed them, and the safeguards you commit to before going further. You get to learn what's actually workable in practice.

But I don't think voluntary commitments are sufficient on their own. The obvious issue is that they're voluntary. A company can revise them, interpret them generously, or just not adopt one. Even if every lab acting in good faith had a strong framework, you'd still have competitive pressure pushing people to cut corners, and you'd have no external check on whether a company is following its own policy. So ultimately I'd like to see government regulation that takes the best ideas from these frameworks and makes them binding, ideally with some independent verification, so it's not just "trust us."

The way I'd frame it is that voluntary policies can be a kind of prototype. If several companies converge on similar approaches, like testing for dangerous capabilities in areas such as bioweapons or cyber, and scaling up security and deployment protections as models get more capable, that gives policymakers a much more concrete starting point. It shows the measures are feasible and don't require shutting down the industry. Then regulation can raise the floor so that everyone, including the actors who'd never sign up voluntarily, meets some baseline.

There's also a transparency piece that I think is underrated. Even before you have detailed rules, requiring companies to publish their safety frameworks and report on how they're following them would help a lot. It lets the public, researchers, and governments see what's going on and compare approaches, and it creates accountability if a company says one thing and does another.

So I'd say: voluntary frameworks are useful now, especially for learning and setting norms, but they're a stepping stone. The end state I'd hope for is thoughtful, adaptable regulation informed by what we've learned from them.

r001.rationale: The response calls voluntary frameworks complementary to regulation and says regulation should incorporate their best ideas and make them binding.

r002.rationale: It describes voluntary policies as a prototype where companies can test workable concepts, giving policymakers a concrete starting point for later regulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of something like the Responsible Scaling Policy as being, in a sense, a prototype. The way I'd put it is: we're a company, we've made a set of commitments about how we'll evaluate our models for dangerous capabilities and what safeguards we'll have in place before we train or deploy models past certain thresholds. And that's useful on its own — it binds us, it forces us to actually build the evaluations and the security practices rather than just talking about them. But it's clearly not sufficient as the final answer, because a voluntary commitment only binds the people who've made it, and it only binds them as much as they choose to keep being bound.

So where I see it fitting in is as a kind of testing ground. Right now, nobody really knows how to write good regulation for this, because the technology is moving fast and a lot of the hard questions — what counts as a dangerous capability, how do you measure it, what does "adequate security" actually mean — are things you have to work out by doing them. If a few labs go and try to answer those questions in practice, make mistakes, revise their frameworks, that produces something concrete that policymakers can look at and say, "OK, this part worked, this part was too vague, this is what the gaps were." I'd much rather regulators be able to borrow from something that's been tried than have to invent it from scratch under time pressure.

The other thing I'd say is that one of the biggest failure modes for voluntary frameworks is the competitive pressure. If you're the only one holding yourself to a standard, and you pause while a competitor doesn't, that's a real cost, and it creates pressure to interpret your own commitments loosely. Regulation is the thing that fixes that, because it levels the field — everyone has to meet the same bar. So I actually think the people who work on these frameworks inside labs should want regulation, because it takes away that dynamic.

I'd just add that I don't think the goal should be for the government to copy an RSP verbatim. Our framework is designed for one company's situation, and some of it is going to be wrong. The hope is more that the structure — identify capability thresholds, define what safeguards have to be in place before you cross them, make it verifiable from outside — is a reasonable shape for policy to take, and that the details get hammered out with a lot more input than any one lab can provide.

r001.rationale: It describes voluntary commitments as useful on their own but insufficient as the final answer, with regulation needed to set a common bar—framing them as a supplement to regulation.

r002.rationale: It calls voluntary frameworks a testing ground and says policymakers can use what labs learn to shape regulation.

astra-6.text:
I think voluntary frameworks can be useful as a first step. Companies can make concrete commitments about how they’ll evaluate their models, what safeguards they’ll put in place, and what would cause them to pause development or deployment. That gives governments something to scrutinise and learn from while they’re building their own capacity.

But I wouldn’t want voluntary commitments to be the endpoint. The concern is that, as competition gets more intense, doing the right thing could become costly. You want a baseline that applies to everyone, with independent oversight and consequences for failing to meet it.

So ideally there’s a feedback loop: companies develop and test safety practices, governments learn which ones are meaningful, and regulation makes the essential protections mandatory. You need enough flexibility to adapt as the technology changes, without making the commitments so flexible that they stop being commitments.

r001.rationale: It presents voluntary commitments as a first step that informs governments, while saying essential protections should ultimately be mandatory through regulation.

r002.rationale: It says companies can develop and test safety practices for governments to assess, with meaningful protections later made mandatory by regulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think voluntary frameworks can be a useful first step, especially when the technology is moving faster than governments can develop detailed rules. Companies can make concrete commitments about how they’ll evaluate their models, what would trigger additional safeguards, and when they would decide not to deploy. That gives regulators something to examine and learn from.

But I wouldn’t want voluntary commitments to be the endpoint. If taking a precaution is costly, you don’t want a system where the companies that take safety most seriously are consistently at a competitive disadvantage. Government regulation can establish a floor that applies to everyone.

The challenge is figuring out which parts to formalise. I’d want companies to be quite specific about their evaluations and decision-making, while leaving room to update the technical details as we learn more. And there needs to be some independent way of checking whether those commitments are actually being followed. Otherwise, a framework can look reassuring without changing very much.

r001.rationale: It presents voluntary commitments as a useful first step and says government regulation should set a shared safety floor, framing the frameworks as a supplement rather than a replacement.

r002.rationale: It says regulators can examine and learn from company commitments, but does not clearly describe the frameworks as a testing ground for provisions that could later be incorporated into regulation.
